deep_dive.title: Beyond the Trial-and-Error Loop: Hybrid Projection and Automated Tuning for Distributed Training
deep_dive.abstract: Configuring distributed LLM training across hundreds of GPUs requires jointly optimizing tensor, pipeline, expert, context, and data parallelism alongside micro-batch size, recomputation, sharding, and overlap, a combinatorial space where memory legality can hinge on a single byte of activation accounting. Today, teams navigate it through expensive multi-node trial and error, burning GPU-hours on crashes and suboptimal recipes. We present Primus Projection, which closes this loop with two coupled components. First, a hybrid projection engine that measures what it can and simulates what it cannot: GPU microbenchmarks on as few as a single device capture compute kernels and any in-scope communication; a sub-node downscale-measure-upscale workflow analytically restores out-of-scope collectives, FSDP overlap, and the full pipeline schedule at the multi-node target. A pure simulation mode runs entirely on CPU, enabling pre-silicon planning without any GPU. Second, the Primus Tuning Agent treats the projection engine as a fast scoring oracle (seconds per candidate instead of tens of minutes) and uses it to drive an intelligent search over the configuration space. A deterministic seed planner sweeps single axes; an LLM investigation loop proposes cross-axis combinations the planner cannot reach, with an analytic memory pre-filter that rejects infeasible candidates before any GPU time is spent. Validated on Llama 3.1 (dense) and Mixtral 8x22B (MoE) across two GPU generations, all projections stay within ~10% of measured multi-node throughput, and fidelity holds at production scale: 4.7% error on DeepSeek V3 671B at 1,024 GPUs and 1.9% on Qwen3-235B-A22B at 256 GPUs. In a Mixtral 8x22B case study, the Primus Tuning Agent discovers a configuration delivering +27% throughput over the published 4-node BF16 reference at the same scale, in under 30 minutes of single-node exploration.

deep_dive.title: Eunoia: Toward Application-Transparent, Scalable GPU Sharing in AI-RAN
deep_dive.abstract: The AI-RAN paradigm makes the next-generation cellular network more versatile by co-locating AI and RAN workloads on the same commodity hardware. While the GPU is a promising platform for AI-RAN realization, a generic concurrent AI application interferes with the latency-sensitive RAN on GPU compute resources. In this paper, we propose Eunoia, a dynamic real-time AI-RAN GPU scheduler that is transparent to both AI applications and the RAN workload and operates at the granularity level of the RAN slot. We deploy Eunoia onto NVIDIA Aerial AI-RAN and evaluate Eunoia on both an over-the-air 5G private network and an emulated multi-cell network. We demonstrate that in a 27-cell AI-RAN, Eunoia keeps the RAN uplink P99 latency under 3 ms while delivering higher AI performance than other RAN-safe static partitioning methods.

deep_dive.title: Stable Token-level Scheduling for Serverless LLM Inference
deep_dive.abstract: Serverless inference is emerging as an efficient deployment model for Large Language Models (LLMs) due to its ability to elastically scale resources, improve GPU utilization through resource sharing, and reduce infrastructure costs. However, existing approaches primarily optimize time to first token (TTFT) while overlooking inter-token latency (ITL), a key determinant of user experience during response generation. We observe that LLM inference comprises a computation-intensive prefill stage and a bandwidth-bound decode stage, where admitting new requests can disrupt ongoing decoding and increase latency. To address this, we propose Token Window Pacing (TWP), a closed-loop scheduling framework that leverages runtime feedback from ITL, queue depth, and workload characteristics to regulate request admission at the token level instead of the batch level. TWP dynamically adjusts a selfregulating token window and incorporates chunk-based prefill to minimize interference from incoming requests. Experiments on realistic serverless workloads show that TWP delivers stable TTFT, significantly reduces latency spikes, lowers P99 tail latency, minimizes ITL variation, and improves throughput by up to 45% over ServerlessLLM and 58% over conventional schedulers. These results demonstrate that feedback-driven tokenlevel scheduling enables stable, high-throughput serverless LLM inference without modifying the underlying model.

deep_dive.title: Scaling LLM Inference via Parallelism: Throughput-Latency Trade-off
deep_dive.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) serving systems must balance latency and throughput while efficiently utilizing distributed GPU resources. This challenge arises because inference consists of two fundamentally different phases: prefill, which determines time-to-first-token (TTFT), and decode, which determines inter-token latency (ITL). The use of tensor parallelism (TP), pipeline parallelism (PP), and hybrid configurations exposes different trade-offs between these latency dimensions, making the optimal parallelism configuration highly dependent on workload characteristics, latency requirements, and context length. Moreover, despite the widespread adoption of distributed inference, there is still limited understanding of how parallelism configurations should be selected under varying workload conditions and service-level objectives (SLO). In this paper, we develop a systematic framework for characterizing LLM inference parallelism via throughput-latency trade-offs, SLO-aware serving, and long-context scalability. We introduce the notion of parallelism operating regions by constructing TTFT-ITL feasible sets and Pareto frontiers across different workload compositions, thereby revealing a systematic transition from TP-dominant to PP-dominant configurations as workloads become increasingly prefill-heavy. We further formulate SLO-aware parallelism selection using goodput, showing that stringent TTFT requirements favor PP-dominated configurations, whereas relaxed latency constraints progressively shift the optimality toward TP-dominated configurations with higher serving capacity. Finally, we demonstrate that increasing context length fundamentally changes the relative advantages of parallelism configurations, with PP-dominant configurations exhibiting more favorable scalability and SLO attainment in the long-context regime.

deep_dive.title: Energy-Aware Agentic Orchestration for Multi-Site Service Deployment
deep_dive.abstract: Energy-aware orchestration across geographically distributed infrastructures is increasingly important as data centers absorb growing Artificial Intelligence (AI) workloads. However, existing approaches often exclude the energy cost of automated decision-making from system-level sustainability assessments. This paper presents an energy-aware agentic orchestration framework that treats Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning as a measurable component of the control loop. We compare single-shot tool calling, ReAct, and plan-and-execute strategies on a multi-site Kubernetes testbed spanning two European data centers and instrumented at layers ranging from power distribution units to per-pod energy attribution. Using ten natural-language orchestration intents with varying decision complexity, we show that reasoning strategy and intent complexity strongly influence graphics processing unit (GPU) energy consumption during orchestration decisions. ReAct and plan-and-execute generated executable tool calls across all evaluated intents but required multiple LLM inferences, whereas the single-shot configuration was less costly but non-actionable. Prefix caching reduced mean ReAct GPU energy consumption by 29.4%. For the evaluated lightweight workload, the infrastructure-energy changes observed within the one-second measurement window were insufficient to offset the measured GPU decision energy. These findings demonstrate the importance of accounting for reasoning overhead when assessing the sustainability of AI-native orchestration and motivate energy-budgeted selection of agent strategies.

deep_dive.title: A New Lens on Multi-GPU Communication: API-Level Memory Models for Portable Optimization
deep_dive.abstract: As network communication increasingly becomes a performance bottleneck for ML and HPC workloads, it is more important than ever to optimize multi-GPU data transfers. Recently, low-level device APIs have emerged that allow programmers to perform fine-grain optimizations via one-sided put/get operations triggered directly from the device. However, the communication libraries providing these device APIs (e.g., rocSHMEM, MSCCL++, and NCCL/RCCL GIN) currently lack a rigorous memory model defining how their primitives interact with the underlying memory systems. Without this, emerging HPC and ML workloads aggressively optimizing network communication via device APIs can be brittle, error-prone, and face compatibility and inter-operability challenges.   This paper proposes the use of API-level memory models for these emerging device communication APIs. An API-level memory model defines the memory semantics of communication API calls in a way that abstracts lower-level details from the API user and simplifies development. This work defines one such model for device-side communication (implemented in AMD's recently open sourced rocSHMEM library) and demonstrates how formal relaxations to such a model can enable low-level LLM performance optimizations while retaining a well-defined standardized interface. Specifically, we describe how updating the SHMEM API implemented by rocSHMEM can properly support cache bypassing for network data, improving performance of a collective communication workload by up to 2.48x, a fused compute+communication workload by up to 1.77x, and a state-of-the-art expert-parallel communication workload by up to 1.18x.

quick_skim.title: MODAIC: Coordinated Asynchrony for Decentralized Multimodal Learning
quick_skim.abstract: Multimodal decentralized learning enables collaboration across heterogeneous edge devices without sharing raw data, but differing modality sets create coupled computation and communication bottlenecks. Multimodal agents support cross-modal alignment while training more model components and sharing bandwidth across multiple modality overlays. Under bandwidth limits, these agents can become hot spots: transfers miss aggregation windows, and their updates become stale or underrepresented, degrading worst-agent accuracy. Asynchrony removes global blocking but does not by itself coordinate local cross-modal interaction with timely peer-update exchange. We present MODAIC (Modality-Decoupled Asynchrony with Interleaved Coordination), a wait-free system that coordinates local modality progress, peer-to-peer update delivery, and aggregation under heterogeneous compute and bandwidth. Hierarchical asynchrony lets modalities progress independently while enforcing reciprocal feature exchange; load-aware update fetching overlaps training with communication, limits concurrent serving load, and reuses late arrivals; and consensus-aware peer selection uses lightweight metadata to account for update availability, peer participation, and loss similarity without active probing. We implement MODAIC as a containerized multi-agent framework and evaluate it on local and cross-region cloud testbeds. Across AVE and KU-HAR, MODAIC improves average accuracy and multimodal worst-agent performance. On AVE at 200 Mbps per agent, it improves multimodal worst-agent accuracy by 11.0 percentage points at 1000 seconds over the strongest baseline. On the cloud testbed, it reduces time-to-accuracy by up to 30%. Ablations show that simpler load-balancing and delayed-aggregation variants leave a worst-agent accuracy gap, and stress tests show tolerance to WAN variability and partial tracker unavailability.

quick_skim.title: Decentralized collaborative continual learning: A multi-objective minimization-based technique
quick_skim.abstract: In this work, we formulate decentralized continual learning within a multi-objective optimization framework. For a given inference task t (corresponding to a common minimizer shared by the cost functions of all agents), agents collecting data in a distributed and streamed manner are only allowed to perform local computations and to exchange information with neighboring agents over the underlying communication graph. As tasks evolve sequentially over time, agents must adapt to newly arriving tasks while retaining knowledge acquired from previously learned ones. This requirement leads to the wellknown stability plasticity dilemma, where stability refers to the ability to retain previous knowledge, while plasticity refers to the ability to learn and adapt to new tasks. To address the stability challenge, agents store subsets of samples from past tasks in local memory buffers. Then, through an appropriate multiobjective formulation, the stored information is incorporated into the learning process so that parameter updates account jointly for the current task and previously learned tasks. The proposed decentralized continual learning approach is analyzed in the mean square error sense under general assumptions on the individual cost functions and gradient noise processes. The analysis reveals that cooperation among agents improves the performance of continual learning. In particular, by exchanging information with neighboring agents, decentralized collaborative learning can exploit the diversity of locally observed data and memory buffers to improve the network average mean-square deviation (MSD) across tasks. Finally, simulations illustrate the theoretical findings and the effectiveness of the method in reducing forgetting and improving the average MSD across tasks.

quick_skim.title: EDiS: Edge Disjoint Subgraph Sparsification Framework for Graph Neural Networks
quick_skim.abstract: Sparse GNN training reduces computation, but deciding which edges to keep can be costly. Reusing one sparse graph is cheap, but locks training to a fixed topology, while varying it across epochs can require repeated sampling or recomputation. We introduce EDiS (Edge-Disjoint Subgraph sparsification framework), which separates one-time structural extraction from per-epoch graph composition. EDiS decomposes the graph once into cacheable edge-disjoint subgraphs, then recombines them into graphs with edge-budget constraints across epochs and retention ratios without re-extracting structure. Our default construction uses feature-based scores and successive maximum score covering forests, while the same composition mechanism also supports alternative edge selection rules. We provide a combinatorial analysis of the per-epoch sampler, the composition step that draws a training graph from the cached decomposition. We show that, under the default covering-forest selector, the stored decomposition deterministically preserves high-score cut edges, and we derive a selector-agnostic conditional bound on high-score cut survival in composed training graphs. Across 19 homophilic, heterophilic, and large-scale node classification benchmarks against 17 baselines under the same edge budget, EDiS achieves the highest mean benchmark score (accuracy/ROC-AUC) and the lowest average rank and gap-to-best among ranked methods. Ablations show the clearest benefits of structural decomposition and epoch variation at tight edge budgets.

quick_skim.title: Best of Both Worlds in Federated LSA: Speedup When Possible, Personalization Always
quick_skim.abstract: We study personalized federated linear stochastic approximation (LSA), a framework which notably encompass personalized temporal difference learning. In this setting, heterogeneous agents collaborate to solve distinct linear fixed-point equations, each corresponding to an agent-specific learning problem. A central open question in personalized learning is whether a single method can adapt to an unknown level of heterogeneity by converging to each agent's personalized solution in all regimes while achieving a linear speedup in the number of agents when their learning problems are sufficiently similar. We answer this question affirmatively by introducing PF-LSA, a minimalist algorithm that mixes each agent's local stochastic update with the average update across agents, at no additional computational cost relative to standard federated methods. We prove that PF-LSA, achieves best-of-both-worlds guarantees without any prior knowledge on the level of heterogeneity. Our analysis is based on a sharp decomposition of the error into consensus and disagreement components. The consensus error decays rapidly, whereas the disagreement error decays more slowly but becomes negligible in low-heterogeneity regimes.

quick_skim.title: Shared Low-rank Basis Factorization for Data-free Mixture-of-Experts Compression
quick_skim.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models decouple capacity from compute through sparse routing, but their large parameter count creates storage and serving challenges. We analyze three MoE compression families: expert pruning, expert merging, and weight reconstruction, and derive structural error bounds showing that pruning and merging can incur non-vanishing errors tied to routing and expert heterogeneity. In contrast, weight reconstruction avoids these structural costs by preserving expert structure and routing. Motivated by the analysis, we propose Shared Low-rank Basis Factorization (SLBF), a data-free weight reconstruction method that uses rank-$k$ bases shared among experts, enabling richer cross-expert sharing, faster convergence, and lower reconstruction error. A post-hoc gauge fixing removes redundant parameters at no representational cost. Across five MoE architectures spanning 16B to 122B parameters, SLBF consistently outperforms methods from all three compression families.

quick_skim.title: BLEND: Balancing Personalization vs. Generalization in Federated Vision-Language Models
quick_skim.abstract: Federated vision-language models (FedVLMs) represent one of the emerging frontiers of machine learning, aiming to integrate federated learning within the fine-tuning pipelines of vision-language models (VLMs). In this work, we introduce BLEND, a new framework designed to jointly enhance the personalization and generalization capabilities of FedVLMs. BLEND proposes a selective VLM parameter fine-tuning and aggregation strategy that consists of (i) global vision and text adapters shared across clients, and (ii) a personalized vision projection adapter tailored to each client. BLEND further introduces a novel loss function that blends the outputs of the global and personalized adapters to achieve personalization, while simultaneously promoting generalization through a principled anchor design implemented via the projection heads of the zero-shot VLM. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BLEND consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, highlighting its ability to effectively balance personalization and generalization across diverse system settings. (Code is available at: https://github.com/payamsiabd/BLEND.git)

quick_skim.title: AutoAdapt: Automatic Domain Discovery Enables Low-Cost Extensibility
quick_skim.abstract: Instruction-tuned models are deployed into environments where domains are heterogeneous and evolve, yet adding new domains or data typically requires costly retraining. We present AutoAdapt, a modular framework that incorporates new domains and data via targeted single-adapter training without modifying other adapters. The framework automatically discovers latent domains, uses them to train per-domain Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters independently in parallel and performs parameter-free routing. Across 14 domain-specific benchmarks and GPT-4o pairwise judgements, AutoAdapt achieves parity with a LoRA adapter trained on all domains without requiring full-model retraining. We also find evidence of specialisation effect convergence across independent discovery methods. Overall, training each adapter on its own domain prevents domain interference by construction, thus enabling modular, taxonomy-free domain specialisation without aggregate performance loss or full model retraining.

quick_skim.title: ShoreKeeper: Accelerating Iterative Data Analytics in the Cloud via Distributed Recovery-Cost-Aware Caching
quick_skim.abstract: Large-scale data-intensive workloads powered by iterative graph or machine learning processing have an insatiable demand for memory due to the continuous generation of new intermediate data. Although existing caching strategies strive to keep performance-critical data in memory, they often fail in practice because they are limited to node-local memory management and assume high node availability. In this paper, we introduce ShoreKeeper, a framework that maximizes execution efficiency by treating cluster-wide memory as a unified, elastic pool. ShoreKeeper employs a global optimization model that maps distributed dataflows into a single graph abstraction to minimize the recovery cost of data evicted from cache across the cluster. To handle memory working sets and cluster capacities that fluctuate over time, ShoreKeeper employs a graph-pruning technique that permits the fast refinement of the caching plan. These optimizations allow ShoreKeeper to work seamlessly whether deployed on highly available VMs or cost-effective preemptible instances in the cloud. Our experiments show that ShoreKeeper consistently outperforms state-of-the-art systems.

quick_skim.title: Private and Distributionally Robust Federated Multiclass Classification
quick_skim.abstract: Fault diagnosis in asset-intensive industries requires multiclass models trained on noisy, sensitive data collected across geographically distributed client sites. Federated learning enables collaborative training without centralizing data, but most approaches do not provide formal privacy guarantees for individual records stored at client sites and can degrade under label noise. To address these limitations, we develop a differentially private, distributionally robust framework for federated multiclass classification that provides sample-level privacy for records stored at each client. We build on a federated Wasserstein distributionally robust multiclass objective with the Crammer-Singer loss, solved using an Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM)-based algorithm. To protect the released client updates, our method injects calibrated Gaussian noise into the proximal linearized client updates of both the local model and the local distributionally robust variable before aggregation at the central server, and we quantify the cumulative privacy loss using the moments accountant. We provide per-round sample-level $(ε,δ)$-differential privacy guarantees and an overall composed privacy guarantee across all training rounds, together with convergence results and an explicit privacy-utility tradeoff. Experiments on simulated industrial fault data and UCI benchmark datasets show that our method outperforms differentially private federated empirical risk minimization and stochastic gradient descent baselines in most tested settings, with the largest gains under strong privacy-induced noise.

quick_skim.title: On the Depth Transfer of Neural Optimizers via L-Smoothness
quick_skim.abstract: Scaling deep learning models efficiently requires predictable performance transfer across compute regimes. Establishing reliable hyperparameter transfer allows optimal training dynamics and structural choices to be discovered on low-cost proxy models, avoiding catastrophic failures during massive-scale training. Existing depth-transfer analyses are architecture-specific and heuristic: hyperparameter transfer is only justified through toy blocks, and both rely on infinite-depth dynamics, a specific initialization, and feature-learning criteria. Building on $L$-smoothness framework of Xu et al. (2026), we understand hyperparameter transfer as how do the Lipschitz and $L$-smoothness constants of the loss scale with the depth $K$? We show that inverse-depth residual branch scaling $α=Θ(1/K)$ is sufficient to make both constants depth-independent at fixed width, uniformly over the bounded parameter domain and for arbitrary $p\to q$ geometries. Because the bounds depend on each residual branch only through its Lipschitz and smoothness constants, the argument applies to general residual networks (including branches of block depth $\geq 2$ such as transformer and ResNet blocks) without assumptions on initialization or correlations between layer weights. Since the smoothness constant controls the curvature penalty in the descent inequality, our bounds motivate a learning-rate scale without an additional depth-dependent curvature correction for updates bounded in the prescribed norm. This provides a geometric explanation of inverse-depth residual scaling and its application to the operator-norm geometries associated with AdamW, Muon, and MOGA. Learning-rate sweeps on GPT-2 (depths 2--128) and CIFAR-100 ResNets (8--32 residual blocks) confirm that Muon and MOGA exhibit stable learning-rate transfer under these prescriptions, with a common optimal rate across a 64-fold increase in depth.

quick_skim.llm_tldr_cn: 大模型训练若无法将小规模代理实验中的优化器配置可靠迁移到更深网络，往往需要高成本试错，并可能在大规模训练时出现失稳。本文以损失函数的L光滑性和Lipschitz常数随网络深度的缩放关系来刻画深度迁移。作者据此分析逆深度残差等结构下的优化器超参数规律，摆脱既有分析对特定结构和无限深度假设的依赖。该理论为大规模模型训练中的低成本调参与稳定扩展提供了方法支撑。

quick_skim.title: Heterogeneous Structured Pruning Under Resource Constraints for Hardware-Efficient Large Language Models
quick_skim.abstract: Training-free pruning removes weights from pretrained large language models to reduce their deployment cost. However, existing approaches typically consider only the total number of retained weights. Consequently, their pruning decisions do not account for how target hardware stores and processes those weights. These methods select a sparsity structure in advance and apply it uniformly to all projections, rather than accounting for how each structure trades pruning error against latency and memory across sublayers. We propose Heterogeneous Structured Pruning (HSP), a hardware-aware pruning framework that combines two components: (i) a heterogeneous search space of dense, unstructured, 2:4, block-sparse, and head / channel (H/C) pruning options and (ii) structure-regularising constraints based on latency and memory models. Our contribution generalises existing importance-based methods: a global solver selects one option per sublayer to minimise proxy pruning loss under a resource budget, thereby assigning each projection a structure and density. We evaluate HSP on OPT and LLaMA models for an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super edge device, where it improves the quality-resource frontiers over training-free baselines.   A project page and updated links for the related code is maintained at: cameronbarker.me/publications/hsp.

quick_skim.llm_tldr_en: HSP optimizes heterogeneous pruning structures across LLM sublayers according to hardware latency, memory, and accuracy tradeoffs, providing a deployment-oriented optimization method relevant to efficient AI infrastructure.
quick_skim.llm_tldr_cn: 预训练大语言模型的剪枝通常只控制保留参数量，忽略不同硬件对稀疏结构的存储和执行差异，因而难以同时优化时延、内存与精度。论文提出硬件感知的异构结构化剪枝框架，在不同子层选择稠密、非结构化、二选四、块稀疏及头或通道等结构。该设计按层权衡剪枝误差与硬件资源代价，而非采用统一稀疏模式。工作为受资源限制的模型部署和AI基础设施效率优化提供实用方法。
